doc.title: Donn Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 6, 2009

title: Drinking age, isolation and tuition
summary: Drinking age of 18, weekend trips to girls' schools, and tuition of about eleven hundred dollars with room and board.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: It was 18? And then it went up?
I don’t know when. That’s why —
No, no, no, I’m wrong. It’s 21 now. It changed in the early 80s or something.

And New York was one of the last to change as I recall. It was no problem with that. In fact I would venture to say that some of the drinking at colleges today is perhaps because of the age limit. You know they sneak around and they get perhaps a little more than they should. And there’s trouble. But most of the guys here, because it’s an isolated school, if we had a house party and people were drinking, it was here. It stayed here. It’s kind of like what happens in Vegas stays in Vegas. Well same thing here at Hamilton. If you went down the hill you might not come back up.
At the time did you feel like it was isolated here?

Yeah sometimes I did, in good weather anyway. Friday afternoons somebody would say, “rollin’” or “wheels up” and off we would go to Skidmore or Wells. Ninety miles, it didn’t matter. Sometimes we even went to Cazenovia.
Yes it was. It may still be, I don’t know. It was a junior college then.
Do you remember what your tuition was in those years?

Let’s see. The figure 7 hundred dollars for tuition strikes a bell. And that, coupled with the room and board, which was a whole different billing, ended up to be around 11 hundred, 12 hundred dollars. And I was on a half tuition scholarship, and I had a job in the fraternity the whole time I was here doing one thing or another. So it was about eleven hundred, and as Phil said today in his speech, next year’s tuition and board and room is 49 thousand. That’s a hunk of change. But even then you know, 11 hundred dollars was not exorbitant, certainly. But it was still cheaper to go to a public college or a university.
